content.content:
1	# ChronicleFlow
2	
3	ChronicleFlow is a small backend for durable workflow orchestration. It stores
4	workflow definitions, execution state, and an append-only event history in
5	SQLite so an execution can be inspected and replayed deterministically.
6	
7	The initial release intentionally supports a compact public contract:
8	
9	- workflows are directed acyclic graphs of `task`, `condition`, and bounded
10	  `loop` nodes;
11	- a workflow may declare named versions: every declared version is kept and
12	  each execution is bound to the version that was current (or explicitly
13	  named) when it started, so upgrading a workflow never changes a running
14	  execution, and a running execution can be explicitly migrated to another
15	  version of the same workflow, after which it advances under that version;
16	- executions advance one ready task at a time, evaluating conditions and
17	  skipping unmatched branches automatically;
18	- task nodes may declare a bounded number of retries: a submitted failure
19	  re-queues the node until the retries are exhausted, which terminates the
20	  execution;
21	- a task node may declare an approval point with the people allowed to decide
22	  it; advancing parks the task in a waiting state until an approver approves
23	  (completing it with the submitted output) or rejects (terminating the
24	  execution with reason `rejected`);
25	- executions may declare a timeout in seconds, after which they terminate and
26	  no longer accept output, and they may be cancelled explicitly;
27	- loop nodes repeat their body a bounded number of times, re-evaluating a
28	  continue condition at the loop boundaries;
29	- every state transition is appended to the execution event stream;
30	- replay rebuilds execution state from the recorded events;
31	- a checkpoint is written at every node boundary, capturing the state
32	  summary and event position, so an execution can be recovered from the
33	  latest checkpoint after a restart;
34	- workers may claim a running execution to receive a work item with a
35	  time-bounded lease, renew the lease with heartbeats, and release it;
36	  while a lease is active only its holder may submit results, and an
37	  expired or released lease returns the work item to the claimable set;
38	- duplicate commands with the same idempotency key return the original result;
39	- workflows and executions may declare webhook subscriptions, and matching
40	  business events are delivered to the declared targets with bounded retries,
41	  each delivery recorded in a per-execution history;
42	- a workflow may declare a schedule — a fixed interval in seconds or a
43	  five-field cron plan — and the service automatically creates one execution
44	  per due period with the declared input; schedules can be paused and
45	  resumed, and periods missed while paused are either caught up once or
46	  skipped, according to the declared missed policy.
47	
48	## Requirements
49	
50	- Python 3.11 or newer
51	- no third-party runtime dependencies
52	
53	## Run the service
54	
55	```bash
56	PYTHONPATH=src python -m chronicleflow.server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --database chronicleflow.db
57	```
58	
59	The process prints `ChronicleFlow listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080` after it
60	has bound the port.
61	
62	## HTTP API
63	
64	All request and response bodies are JSON. Unknown fields are rejected.
65	
66	Responses are compact JSON with no insignificant whitespace, and every
67	response body ends with exactly one trailing newline (`\n`). Numbers
68	round-trip with their full precision: finite floats keep their original
69	IEEE-754 value through the shortest textual representation that decodes to
70	it (so `0.30000000000000004` stays `0.30000000000000004`), negative zero is
71	preserved as `-0.0`, and integers stay integers. Non-finite numbers may
72	never appear in a request and are never produced in a response; timestamps
73	are ISO-8601 UTC strings ending in `Z`.
74	
75	### Tenants and quotas
76	
77	A request may declare a tenant by sending the `X-Tenant-Id` header with a
78	non-empty identifier. Every workflow, execution, schedule, schedule status,
79	and delivery history record is scoped to the tenant of the request that
80	created it: queries and operations only ever see data belonging to that
81	tenant, and different tenants may use the same workflow or execution
82	identifiers without colliding. Referencing another tenant's resource — for
83	example advancing, migrating, deciding, claiming, cancelling, recovering, replaying, or
84	reading the events, checkpoints, deliveries, or schedule of an execution or
85	workflow owned by another tenant — is answered exactly like a reference to a
86	missing resource: `404 not_found`, with no indication that the resource
87	exists elsewhere. An execution created in one tenant can only reference a
88	workflow of the same tenant, and a migration can only name a version of that
89	workflow in the same tenant; referencing an unseen workflow identifier or
90	version is the usual `404 not_found`.
91	
92	The header applies to every workflow, execution, and schedule entry point,
93	including creation, advancement, migration, approval decisions, lease
94	operations, cancellation, recovery, replay, and all history and status
95	queries. An empty
96	`X-Tenant-Id` value is a `400 validation_error`. Requests that omit the
97	header entirely keep using the single legacy namespace, whose advancement,
98	approvals, leases, retries, timeouts, cancellation, checkpoints, recovery,
99	scheduling, and replay behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged: the tenant is
100	stored only as database scope, never added to a state field or event payload,
101	and state shapes and event streams gain no new fields. Idempotency keys are
102	scoped per tenant as well, so tenants can never see or collide with each
103	other's keys; reusing a key for another operation within the same tenant is
104	the usual `409 conflict`.
105	
106	A tenant may declare quotas bounding how many workflows and executions it may
107	hold:
108	
109	```http
110	PUT /quotas
111	Idempotency-Key: quota-request-1
112	X-Tenant-Id: acme
113	
114	{"workflows": 10, "executions": 100}
115	```
116	
117	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must contain exactly
118	`workflows` and `executions`, each a positive integer; a non-positive,
119	non-integer, boolean, or non-finite value, a missing or extra field, or a
120	non-object body is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Both quota
121	routes require a tenant: calling them without `X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty
122	one) is a `400 validation_error`. The response is
123	`{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100}}`; declaring again replaces the
124	limits (re-anchoring nothing else). Lowering a limit below the current
125	holding deletes no existing data — existing workflows and executions stay
126	fully usable — it only rejects later writes that would exceed the new limit.
127	
128	```http
129	GET /quotas
130	X-Tenant-Id: acme
131	```
132	
133	Returns the declared quota, or the definite empty result `{"quota":null}`
134	when the tenant has declared none.
135	
136	When a write would take the tenant past either limit, the whole request is
137	rejected with `409 conflict` and an error message that names the quota (for
138	example `quota exceeded: tenant already holds 10 workflows (quota limit is
139	10)`), so callers can tell quota rejection apart from an ordinary identifier
140	conflict. The rejection performs no partial write: nothing is inserted and
141	previously stored data is unaffected, exactly as for validation failures.
142	
143	A schedule firing on time creates its execution in the schedule's tenant and
144	that execution counts against the tenant's execution quota. When the tenant
145	is at its execution limit, the due period creates no execution and the
146	schedule is left unchanged — its cursor, `last_triggered_at`, and
147	`last_execution_id` stay as they were — so the period is settled on a later
148	pass once capacity exists, under the usual per-period idempotence. Delivery
149	history follows the tenant of the execution it belongs to.
150	
151	### Health
152	
153	```http
154	GET /health
155	```
156	
157	Returns `{"status":"ok"}`.
158	
159	### Create a workflow
160	
161	```http
162	POST /workflows
163	Idempotency-Key: workflow-request-1
164	
165	{
166	  "id": "order-flow",
167	  "nodes": [
168	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
169	    {"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
170	  ]
171	}
172	```
173	
174	Returns HTTP 201 with the stored workflow. Node identifiers must be unique,
175	dependencies must exist, and cycles are rejected.
176	
177	A workflow definition may carry an optional `version` tag; declaring one
178	enables upgrades and keeps every version. Versioning is described under
179	"Workflow versions" below, and a workflow's stored versions and current
180	version are available through `GET /workflows/{id}`.
181	
182	A workflow may also declare webhook `subscriptions` alongside its nodes:
183	
184	```json
185	{
186	  "id": "order-flow",
187	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
188	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/orders", "events": ["execution_completed"]}]
189	}
190	```
191	
192	See "Webhook notifications" below for the subscription shape and delivery
193	semantics; the subscriptions apply to every execution of the workflow (for a
194	versioned workflow, to executions bound to that version).
195	
196	A workflow may also declare a `schedule` alongside its nodes:
197	
198	```json
199	{
200	  "id": "nightly-orders",
201	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
202	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"}
203	}
204	```
205	
206	See "Schedules" below for the declaration shape and the trigger semantics.
207	
208	Besides `task`, a node may have `kind` set to `condition`:
209	
210	```json
211	{"id": "is_vip", "kind": "condition", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "path": "customer.vip", "equals": true}
212	```
213	
214	`path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into the execution input and `equals`
215	is a JSON scalar (string, number, boolean, or null). A condition is evaluated
216	automatically once its dependencies complete: the input value at `path` is
217	compared with `equals` by JSON type and value, and a missing path evaluates to
218	`false`.
219	
220	A task may carry an optional `run_if` guard:
221	
222	```json
223	{"id": "expedite", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["is_vip"], "run_if": {"condition_id": "is_vip", "expected": true}}
224	```
225	
226	`condition_id` must reference a `condition` node that is also listed in the
227	task's `depends_on`. When the condition's result differs from `expected`, the
228	task is marked as skipped: it receives no output and still satisfies the
229	dependencies of its successors.
230	
231	A task may declare how many times it is retried after a failure:
232	
233	```json
234	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "retries": 3}
235	```
236	
237	`retries` is an integer between 0 and 10 and defaults to 0, meaning the task
238	is attempted only once. Each failure submitted through `advance` consumes one
239	attempt; while retries remain, the task returns to the ready set and is
240	advanced again. When a failure arrives with no retries left, the task is
241	permanently failed and the whole execution terminates with termination reason
242	`retries_exhausted`.
243	
244	A task may instead declare an approval point:
245	
246	```json
247	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "approval": {"approvers": ["alice", "bob"]}}
248	```
249	
250	`approval` contains exactly `approvers`, a non-empty array of approver
251	identifier strings without duplicates; an empty list, a duplicate entry, or a
252	non-string entry is a validation error, and only `task` nodes may carry an
253	approval point. When an `advance` reaches a ready task with an approval point,
254	the task does not complete and the submitted output or failure is not
255	consumed: an `approval_requested` event is appended (recording the node, its
256	approvers, and, inside a loop body, the loop id and iteration) and the
257	execution stays `running`, parked in a waiting state returned under
258	`waiting_approval`. Further `advance` calls return the current state without
259	writing output, completing the node, or appending events; only a decision can
260	move the task.
261	
262	### Submit an approval decision
263	
264	```http
265	POST /executions/run-1/decision
266	Idempotency-Key: decision-request-1
267	
268	{"approver":"alice","decision":"approved","output":{"charge_id":"c-3"}}
269	```
270	
271	`decision` is either `approved` or `rejected`. An approved decision carries
272	exactly `approver`, `decision`, and an `output` object; the task completes with
273	that output and its successors become available in the usual way. A rejected
274	decision carries exactly `approver`, `decision`, and a `reason` string; the
275	task is permanently failed (it is listed under `failed_nodes`) and the
276	execution terminates with termination reason `rejected`. Either decision
277	appends an `approval_decided` event with the node, approver, decision, and (on
278	rejection) the reason, and the approval record is kept under `approvals`. A
279	request whose approver is not in the point's approver list is a 409
280	`conflict`, and a malformed body or a decision value other than `approved` or
281	`rejected` is a 400 `validation_error`; neither changes execution state.
282	Repeating the decision that already resolved the most recent approval point —
283	the same approver and decision with the same output or rejection reason —
284	returns the first result and neither advances the node again nor appends
285	another event; any other decision against an execution with no pending
286	approval point is a 409 `conflict`, and deciding a missing execution returns
287	404.
288	
289	While an execution is parked at an approval point it remains `running`, so a
290	cancellation takes effect immediately with the usual `cancelled` termination
291	reason, and a reached timeout terminates it with `timeout`; both dismiss the
292	pending point and the execution then no longer accepts decisions or output.
293	The waiting point, its request and decision events, and the termination
294	reason are rebuilt solely from the event stream on replay, and the parked and
295	decided node boundaries are checkpointed like every other boundary, so
296	waiting points and recorded decisions remain valid after a restart. Approval
297	state is added to an execution only when its workflow declares at least one
298	approval point; workflows without approvals keep exactly the previous state
299	shape and event stream.
300	
301	A node may also have `kind` set to `loop`, describing a bounded repeated
302	segment:
303	
304	```json
305	{"id": "retry", "kind": "loop", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "entry": "attempt", "condition": "keep_trying", "max_iterations": 3}
306	```
307	
308	A loop node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `entry`, `condition`,
309	and `max_iterations`; any other field is rejected as unknown. `entry` names a
310	`task` node, `condition` names a `condition` node, and `max_iterations` is an
311	integer between 1 and 100. The loop body is the repeated segment anchored by
312	the entry task and the condition: it is the entry task, the condition, and
313	every node either anchor reaches through `depends_on`. The two anchors must
314	be connected — the condition gates the entry task (the entry depends on it)
315	or the condition is evaluated after the entry task (it depends on the entry),
316	as in the example above. The body keeps the usual DAG rules and always
317	contains the referenced condition. The loop's own dependencies must be
318	completed or skipped before the first iteration may start, they must not
319	overlap the body, bodies of different loops must not overlap or nest, and
320	nodes outside a body must not depend on nodes inside it (they depend on the
321	loop node instead).
322	
323	When the loop's dependencies are satisfied, the loop evaluates its condition
324	against the execution input (same JSON type and value comparison as condition
325	nodes; a missing path is `false`). If it is `false`, the loop completes with
326	zero iterations and end reason `condition_false`. If it is `true`, the first
327	iteration starts and the body advances one ready task per `advance` call in
328	the usual deterministic order; conditions and `run_if` skips inside the body
329	are re-evaluated every iteration, and task outputs belong only to the current
330	iteration. Once every body node is completed or skipped, the condition is
331	evaluated again: `true` starts the next iteration, `false` ends the loop with
332	`condition_false`, and reaching `max_iterations` ends it with
333	`iteration_limit` after that iteration finishes. Ending the loop completes
334	the loop node and releases the dependencies of its successors.
335	
336	Execution state exposes each loop under `loops`: `status`, the
337	`current_iteration`, one entry per iteration with its own `completed_nodes`,
338	`skipped_nodes`, `condition_results`, and `outputs`, and the single
339	`end_reason` (`condition_false` or `iteration_limit`). The event stream
340	records `iteration_started`, `loop_condition_evaluated`, and `loop_completed`
341	events alongside the usual per-node ones, so replay rebuilds loop state
342	exactly.
343	
344	### Workflow versions
345	
346	A workflow can declare a version tag alongside its nodes:
347	
348	```json
349	{
350	  "id": "order-flow",
351	  "version": "2026-09-25",
352	  "nodes": [
353	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
354	    {"id": "ship", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
355	  ]
356	}
357	```
358	
359	`version` is an optional non-empty string of at most 100 characters, validated
360	like every other identifier. Posting it when the workflow does not yet exist
361	creates the workflow with that version; posting another definition with a new
362	`version` to the same `id` adds a new version without touching the previous
363	ones — the workflow keeps its entire history, and every stored version remains
364	usable. The most recently added version becomes the workflow's current
365	version. Posting a definition without a `version` to an existing workflow
366	still conflicts, and reusing a version tag already stored for the same
367	workflow is a `409 conflict`; either rejection writes nothing.
368	
369	A version declaration may also carry `subscriptions` and a `schedule`,
370	validated exactly like at creation. Subscriptions are attached to the
371	declared version and apply only to executions bound to it; a version without
372	subscriptions replaces none, and other versions' subscriptions stay intact.
373	Declaring a `schedule` on an added version replaces the workflow's single
374	schedule plan in the usual way (re-anchored, pause flag kept).
375	
376	An execution created without an explicit `version` binds to the workflow's
377	current version at the moment it starts:
378	
379	```http
380	POST /executions
381	Idempotency-Key: execution-versioned
382	
383	{"id":"run-v2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{}}
384	```
385	
386	An execution may instead name the version it wants:
387	
388	```json
389	{"id":"run-v1","workflow_id":"order-flow","version":"2026-08-01","input":{}}
390	```
391	
392	Naming a version that does not exist for the workflow is a missing-resource
393	`404 not_found`, exactly like naming a workflow that does not exist; the
394	execution is not created. Everything about an execution follows its bound
395	version: ready-node selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval
396	points, retry counts, leases, and the subscriptions that fire for its events.
397	Adding a new version never interrupts an execution already running: an
398	execution started before the upgrade keeps advancing on its old version to
399	completion or termination. Its checkpoints are snapshots of the same state,
400	recovery rebuilds from the bound version, and replay rebuilds state and the
401	version binding solely from its event stream; recorded events and historical
402	conclusions never change.
403	
404	A versioned execution's state carries its `version` tag, and its
405	`execution_started` event records the same tag; querying it therefore shows
406	which version it is bound to. A workflow that never declares a version, and an
407	execution of one, keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
408	stream with no added field.
409	
410	The definition query lists every version and the current one:
411	
412	```http
413	GET /workflows/order-flow
414	```
415	
416	```json
417	{"current_version":"2026-09-25","id":"order-flow","versions":[
418	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-08-01"},
419	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-09-25"}
420	]}
421	```
422	
423	Versions are returned in declaration order; each entry is the stored
424	definition with its `version` tag. A workflow that never declared a version
425	returns a single untagged entry and `current_version: null`. A missing
426	workflow returns 404 `not_found`. Cross-tenant references are missing
427	resources as usual.
428	
429	### Migrate a running execution to another version
430	
431	```http
432	POST /executions/run-v1/migrate
433	Idempotency-Key: migrate-request-1
434	
435	{"version":"2026-09-25"}
436	```
437	
438	A running execution can be explicitly moved to another declared version of
439	the same workflow; after the call it keeps advancing under the new version.
440	The body must contain exactly `version`, a non-empty version identifier that
441	names a stored version of the execution's workflow. On success a
442	`version_migrated` event is appended to the event stream — it records the
443	`from_version`, the `to_version`, and the structural skeleton of the target
444	revision (its `loops`, and, when it declares approval points, its
445	`waiting_approval` and `approvals` fields) — and a checkpoint of the rebound
446	state is written at that same node boundary. The execution's state then
447	carries the target version.
448	
449	Everything that follows uses the target version's definition: ready-node
450	selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval points, retries, and
451	the workflow subscriptions that fire for later events. Everything recorded
452	before the migration is kept exactly as-is: prior events, node outputs,
453	condition conclusions, and per-iteration history are never rewritten. Loops
454	introduced by the target definition begin in their initial pending state; a
455	loop the old definition knew keeps its recorded iterations and conclusion.
456	Replay rebuilds the migration point and version binding solely from the
457	event stream, and after a restart recovery continues on the migrated version
458	from the migration checkpoint, so checkpoints and materialized state agree.
459	
460	An execution parked at an approval point may also be migrated: the waiting
461	point keeps its recorded node and approver list unchanged (only a recorded
462	approver may still decide it), and once the decision lands the subsequent
463	advancement follows the target version. Executions that are never migrated
464	keep advancing on the version they started with to completion or
465	termination; adding versions never moves them. An execution of a workflow
466	that never declared a version cannot name a target, and such workflows and
467	their executions keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
468	content.
469	
470	The response is the updated execution state. Migrating a `completed` or
471	`terminated` execution returns `409 conflict` and changes nothing. A missing
472	execution or a target version that does not exist for the workflow returns
473	`404 not_found`; a cross-tenant reference is the same missing resource. A
474	missing or mistyped `version`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
475	`400 validation_error`. Migrating to the version the execution is already
476	bound to returns the current state as-is, appending no event and writing no
477	checkpoint; reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a `409
478	conflict`. The migration event is listed directly by the per-execution
479	events query, and node outputs produced after the migration belong to the
480	target version's definition. Approver-list validation, lease renewal, and
481	delivery history keep their existing semantics before and after a migration.
482	
483	### Start an execution
484	
485	```http
486	POST /executions
487	Idempotency-Key: execution-request-1
488	
489	{"id":"run-1","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{"order_id":"o-7"}}
490	```
491	
492	Returns HTTP 201. The execution starts in `running` state. Without an
493	explicit `version`, it binds to the workflow's current version at start time;
494	naming a `version` binds to that one instead (and a missing version is a
495	`404 not_found`). See "Workflow versions" for the binding and upgrade rules.
496	
497	An execution may declare a timeout:
498	
499	```json
500	{"id":"run-2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{},"timeout_seconds":30}
501	```
502	
503	`timeout_seconds` is a positive number of seconds counted from the moment the
504	execution starts. Once the deadline passes, the execution terminates with
505	termination reason `timeout` and no longer accepts output. Executions without
506	a timeout never expire.
507	
508	An execution may also declare its own webhook `subscriptions`, which apply in
509	addition to the ones its workflow declares:
510	
511	```json
512	{
513	  "id": "run-3",
514	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
515	  "input": {},
516	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/ops", "events": ["node_completed"], "max_attempts": 3}]
517	}
518	```
519	
520	### Inspect an execution
521	
522	```http
523	GET /executions/run-1
524	GET /executions/run-1/events
525	GET /executions/run-1/checkpoints
526	```
527	
528	The first endpoint returns the materialized state. The second returns the
529	ordered event stream. The third returns the ordered checkpoints; each entry
530	gives its `sequence`, the `event_sequence` position it was taken at, the full
531	`state` summary, and `created_at`.
532	
533	### Webhook notifications
534	
535	Subscriptions declared on a workflow or an execution deliver outbound webhook
536	messages when business events occur. Each subscription contains exactly:
537	
538	- `url`: a non-empty `http` or `https` address to POST to;
539	- `events`: a non-empty array of event types without duplicates, drawn from
540	  `node_completed`, `execution_completed`, `execution_terminated`, and
541	  `approval_decided` (a termination is the same event type whatever its
542	  reason);
543	- `timeout_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds to wait for each
544	  delivery attempt, defaulting to 5;
545	- `max_attempts` (optional): an integer between 1 and 10, defaulting to 1.
546	
547	Any other field, a missing `url` or `events`, a mistyped value, an empty or
548	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
549	a non-finite number, a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than
550	ten attempts is a 400 `validation_error` and rejects the whole request — no
551	workflow, execution, or subscription is partially written.
552	
553	When a subscribed event occurs, a JSON message is POSTed to each matching
554	target immediately: the body carries `event_type`, `execution_id`, and the
555	event's details (such as `node_id` for a completed node or `approver` for an
556	approval decision). Each delivery request carries an `Idempotency-Key`
557	header; retries of the same event reuse the same key, and different events
558	never share a key. A delivery is attempted at most the subscription's
559	`max_attempts` times, with an increasing backoff between attempts. An
560	unreachable target, a timeout, or a non-2xx response marks the attempt as
561	failed, but a failed delivery never changes the outcome of the call that
562	triggered it.
563	
564	Deliveries do not append execution events, do not add fields to the execution
565	state, and are never triggered by replay, recovery, or queries, so
566	checkpoints and replay conclusions are unaffected. An execution that declares
567	no subscriptions keeps exactly the same state, event stream, and advancement
568	results as before.
569	
570	### Inspect the delivery history
571	
572	```http
573	GET /executions/run-1/deliveries
574	```
575	
576	Returns `{"deliveries": [...]}` in the order the events occurred. Each record
577	gives its `sequence`, the subscription `url`, the `event_type`, the
578	`event_sequence` that triggered it, the delivery `idempotency_key`, the final
579	`status` (`delivered` or `failed`), the `attempt_count`, an `attempts` list
580	recording each try's `status_code` or `error` (so a retry that eventually
581	succeeds is visible attempt by attempt), and `occurred_at`. Querying the
582	history of a missing execution returns 404 `not_found` and records nothing.
583	Every delivery attempt is recorded, including one whose history record itself
584	could not be written: such a failure is not swallowed — it is retried once in
585	a fresh write carrying `status` `failed` and a `persistence_error` describing
586	the write failure, so the attempt remains visible whenever the database can
587	accept it (and is logged rather than silently dropped if it cannot).
588	
589	### Schedules
590	
591	A workflow may declare a schedule so the service creates executions
592	automatically. The declaration happens at workflow creation (a `schedule`
593	field next to `id` and `nodes`) or later through the update endpoint, and it
594	takes effect from the moment it is stored. A schedule contains exactly:
595	
596	- `interval_seconds`: a positive integer number of seconds between runs —
597	  or, alternatively, `cron`: a five-field cron expression (`minute hour
598	  day-of-month month day-of-week`) whose fields support `*`, `*/step`,
599	  single values, ranges `a-b`, ranges with steps `a-b/step`, and
600	  comma-separated lists, with 0 and 7 both meaning Sunday. Exactly one of
601	  `interval_seconds` and `cron` must be present;
602	- `input`: the object used as the execution input of every created run;
603	- `missed_policy`: either `catch_up` or `skip`.
604	
605	Whenever a period of the plan comes due, the service creates one execution
606	for the workflow with the declared input. The created execution is exactly a
607	manually created one: it starts `running` with the same state shape and the
608	usual `execution_started` event, and advancing, approvals, leases, retries,
609	timeouts, and cancellation all behave identically. The trigger itself writes
610	nothing into the created execution's event stream and adds no fields to its
611	state; the schedule's own record of when it fired and which execution it
612	created is exposed through the status query below.
613	
614	Creation is idempotent per schedule period: a repeated trigger or a repeated
615	request for the same period returns the same execution and never creates a
616	second one, under either missed policy. When periods were missed — the
617	schedule was paused, or the service was not running — `catch_up` makes up
618	exactly the single most recent missed period, while `skip` makes up none;
619	neither policy ever creates more than one execution for the same period.
620	
621	An invalid declaration rejects the whole request with 400
622	`validation_error` and writes nothing: a non-positive or non-integer
623	`interval_seconds`, a cron expression with other than five fields, out-of
624	range values, or unparseable fragments, declaring both `interval_seconds`
625	and `cron`, a `missed_policy` other than `catch_up` or `skip`, a missing or
626	mistyped `input`, or any unknown field.
627	
628	### Declare or replace a schedule
629	
630	```http
631	PUT /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
632	Idempotency-Key: schedule-request-1
633	
634	{"interval_seconds":3600,"input":{"mode":"nightly"},"missed_policy":"catch_up"}
635	```
636	
637	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body is validated exactly
638	like a schedule declared at creation time, and the response is the schedule
639	status. Updating replaces the plan and re-anchors it at the update time; the
640	paused flag is kept. A missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`, an invalid
641	plan 400 `validation_error` with no partial write, and reusing an
642	idempotency key from another operation is a 409 `conflict`.
643	
644	### Inspect the schedule status
645	
646	```http
647	GET /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
648	```
649	
650	Returns a single `schedule` object with the status fields, or the definite
651	empty result `{"schedule":null}` for a workflow that never declared a
652	schedule. When a schedule exists the object is:
653	
654	```json
655	{
656	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"},
657	  "paused": false,
658	  "last_triggered_at": "2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z",
659	  "last_execution_id": "nightly-orders-scheduled-i:42"
660	}
661	```
662	
663	The fields are:
664	
665	- `schedule`: the declared plan exactly as stored — either
666	  `{"interval_seconds": <positive integer>, "input": <object>, "missed_policy": "catch_up"|"skip"}`
667	  or `{"cron": "<five-field expression>", "input": <object>, "missed_policy": ...}`;
668	  the input is the declared object verbatim;
669	- `paused`: a JSON boolean;
670	- `last_triggered_at`: an ISO-8601 UTC timestamp string ending in `Z`, or
671	  `null` until the first period fires;
672	- `last_execution_id`: the execution id string of the most recently created
673	  run, or `null` until the first trigger.
674	
675	`last_triggered_at` and `last_execution_id` are `null` (not omitted) until
676	the first trigger. A missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`.
677	
678	### Pause and resume a schedule
679	
680	```http
681	POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/pause
682	Idempotency-Key: pause-request-1
683	
684	{}
685	```
686	
687	```http
688	POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/resume
689	Idempotency-Key: resume-request-1
690	
691	{}
692	```
693	
694	Both bodies must be empty objects; a missing or mistyped body, an unknown
695	field, or a non-finite number is a 400 `validation_error`. While paused, due
696	periods create no executions. Resuming settles the periods that came due
697	during the pause according to the missed policy: `catch_up` immediately
698	creates the single most recent missed run, `skip` creates none. Pausing or
699	resuming a workflow that has no schedule, or any schedule operation on a
700	missing workflow, returns 404 `not_found`; reusing an idempotency key across
701	operations returns 409 `conflict`. Both responses carry the schedule status.
702	
703	Workflows that declare no schedule are unaffected: their creation,
704	advancement, approvals, deliveries, checkpoints, recovery, and replay behave
705	exactly as before, with no additional fields or events.
706	
707	### Checkpoints
708	
709	Every successful `advance` that settles a node boundary — a task is
710	completed, or a failure is submitted (whether it retries or exhausts the
711	attempts) — writes a checkpoint in the same transaction as the state update
712	and event append. The checkpoint stores the complete state summary at that
713	boundary, including completed, skipped, and failed nodes, condition results,
714	outputs, attempts with their unfinished retry counts, and the status and
715	current iteration of every loop (with the per-iteration records), together
716	with the position of the last written event. Because the checkpoint matches
717	the stored state at that position, recovery can continue without replaying or
718	duplicating any node output.
719	
720	Checkpoints do not add fields to the execution state and do not append events:
721	an execution that declares no retries, timeout, or loops keeps exactly the
722	same state shape and event stream as before.
723	
724	### Complete the next ready node
725	
726	```http
727	POST /executions/run-1/advance
728	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-1
729	
730	{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"}}
731	```
732	
733	The lexicographically first ready task is completed. The response contains the
734	updated execution. Before that, each call first evaluates all ready conditions
735	in deterministic order and skips tasks whose `run_if` does not match; if this
736	automatic processing finishes the execution, the current state is returned and
737	the submitted output is not consumed. When every node is completed or skipped,
738	the status becomes `completed`.
739	
740	Instead of an output, a failure can be submitted for the same ready task:
741	
742	```http
743	POST /executions/run-1/advance
744	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-2
745	
746	{"failure":{"reason":"gateway timeout"}}
747	```
748	
749	The body must contain exactly one of `output` or `failure`, and `failure`
750	carries exactly a `reason` string. Either body may additionally carry a
751	`worker_id` string identifying the lease holder when the execution's work
752	item has been claimed (see "Claim a work item"). A failed task appends a `node_failed`
753	event recording the attempt number and reason. While the task has retries
754	left it returns to the ready set and a `node_retried` event records the next
755	attempt number; otherwise the task is permanently failed and the execution
756	terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`. The same rules apply to tasks
757	inside loop bodies, which are retried within their current iteration.
758	
759	Execution state includes `completed_nodes` (which also lists evaluated
760	conditions), `skipped_nodes`, `failed_nodes`, `condition_results`, `outputs`,
761	and `attempts`. `attempts` maps each attempted task to its current `attempt`
762	number and its `failures` count; loop body tasks track the same per iteration.
763	Executions of workflows that declare approval points additionally expose
764	`waiting_approval` (`null`, or the pending point's `node_id`, `approvers`, and
765	loop context) and the `approvals` record list. Each condition evaluation
766	appends a `condition_evaluated` event and each skip a `node_skipped` event to
767	the execution stream.
768	
769	### Cancel an execution
770	
771	```http
772	POST /executions/run-1/cancel
773	Idempotency-Key: cancel-request-1
774	```
775	
776	A running execution is terminated immediately with termination reason
777	`cancelled`. Cancelling a completed or already terminated execution returns
778	its state unchanged, and cancelling a missing execution returns 404.
779	
780	Execution status is `running`, `completed`, or `terminated`. A terminated
781	execution records exactly one `termination_reason` — `retries_exhausted`,
782	`rejected`, `timeout`, or `cancelled` — and appends a single
783	`execution_terminated` event; completed executions keep a `null` termination
784	reason and their own `execution_completed` event. Advancing a terminated
785	execution returns its state unchanged without consuming the submitted output
786	or failure; a decision against one only succeeds as a repeat of the decision
787	that rejected it, and otherwise conflicts.
788	
789	### Claim a work item
790	
791	```http
792	POST /executions/run-1/claim
793	Idempotency-Key: claim-request-1
794	
795	{"worker_id":"worker-7","lease_seconds":30}
796	```
797	
798	Claiming is how an external worker takes ownership of a running execution
799	before advancing its ready tasks. `worker_id` is a non-empty string and
800	`lease_seconds` is an optional positive number of seconds (default 30). The
801	response contains the claimed `work_item` (its `execution_id` and
802	`workflow_id`) and a `lease` recording the `worker_id`, the `lease_seconds`
803	duration, the `expires_at` deadline, and the `heartbeat_at` active time.
804	Each work item is held by at most one worker at a time: claiming a work
805	item whose lease is still active — even by the same worker — is a 409
806	`conflict`. Claiming a completed or terminated execution returns the
807	definite empty result `{"work_item":null,"lease":null}` and absorbs no
808	input, and claiming a missing execution returns 404.
809	
810	While a work item is held, results are submitted through the usual
811	`advance` entry by including the holder's identity:
812	
813	```http
814	POST /executions/run-1/advance
815	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-3
816	
817	{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"},"worker_id":"worker-7"}
818	```
819	
820	Submitting results for a work item held by another worker, or after the
821	lease has expired, is a 409 `conflict` that does not change execution
822	state. An execution that never claimed a work item accepts `advance`
823	exactly as before, and its state fields and event stream are identical to
824	an execution without any claim.
825	
826	When a lease expires, the work item returns to the claimable set and may be
827	claimed again by the same or another worker. The second claim continues
828	from the materialized state: node outputs and results recorded by the
829	earlier holder are never advanced or recorded twice, and every written
830	output belongs to the single advance that submitted it.
831	
832	### Renew a lease
833	
834	```http
835	POST /executions/run-1/heartbeat
836	Idempotency-Key: heartbeat-request-1
837	
838	{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
839	```
840	
841	Within the lease period the holder may heartbeat to extend `expires_at` by
842	the lease duration and refresh the `heartbeat_at` active time; the response
843	carries the updated `lease`. A heartbeat never advances nodes, writes
844	outputs, or appends node events. A heartbeat from another worker or after
845	the lease expired is a 409 `conflict`; a heartbeat for a missing execution
846	or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404 `not_found`.
847	
848	### Release a work item
849	
850	```http
851	POST /executions/run-1/release
852	Idempotency-Key: release-request-1
853	
854	{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
855	```
856	
857	Releasing invalidates the lease immediately and returns the work item to
858	the claimable set, so it can be claimed again right away; progress already
859	made and the recorded events are unchanged. Releasing with another
860	worker's identity or after expiry is a 409 `conflict`; releasing for a
861	missing execution or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404
862	`not_found`.
863	
864	Claims, heartbeats, and releases append no events and add no fields to the
865	execution state, so replay, checkpoints, and recovery are unaffected.
866	Leases live in the same SQLite database as the execution state, so
867	unexpired leases and claim ownership remain valid after the service
868	restarts.
869	
870	### Recover from a checkpoint
871	
872	```http
873	POST /executions/run-1/recover
874	Idempotency-Key: recover-request-1
875	
876	{"from":"latest_checkpoint"}
877	```
878	
879	Recovery rebuilds a running execution from its latest checkpoint and returns
880	the rebuilt execution. It appends no events and changes no state: the rebuilt
881	execution is exactly the materialized state, and a subsequent replay has the
882	same conclusion as before the interruption. After recovery, further
883	`advance` calls continue from the checkpoint, so node outputs, failure
884	reasons, attempt numbers, and loop iteration ownership are identical to an
885	uninterrupted run; failure records for tasks inside a loop body still carry
886	their loop id and current iteration. Recovery works after the service has
887	been restarted, because checkpoints live in the same SQLite database as the
888	execution state and events.
889	
890	A completed execution is returned unchanged, producing no new events. A
891	terminated execution is likewise returned unchanged and the operation
892	absorbs no input; if a timeout or cancellation takes effect between
893	checkpoint writes, termination takes precedence over recovery. Events and
894	checkpoints remain queryable after cancellation or timeout, and their replay
895	stays consistent with the materialized state.
896	
897	Recovering a missing execution returns 404. Recovering an execution that has
898	no checkpoint, or whose latest checkpoint cannot be parsed, returns 409
899	`conflict`. A missing `from` field, a wrong type, or an unknown recovery
900	origin is a 400 `validation_error`; a non-finite number in the body is
901	rejected the same way as every other request. Reusing an idempotency key
902	already used by another operation (including an `advance` or `cancel` on the
903	same execution) returns 409 `conflict`.
904	
905	### Replay
906	
907	```http
908	POST /executions/run-1/replay
909	```
910	
911	Rebuilds state solely from the execution event stream and compares it with the
912	stored materialized state. A successful response contains `consistent: true`
913	and the rebuilt execution.
914	
915	## Errors
916	
917	Errors use this shape:
918	
919	```json
920	{"error":{"code":"validation_error","message":"human readable detail"}}
921	```
922	
923	Validation errors return 400, missing resources return 404, and conflicts
924	return 409. An empty `X-Tenant-Id` header value is a validation error; quota
925	declarations require a tenant and positive integer limits, validated by the
926	same rules as every other body (no non-finite numbers, no unknown fields).
927	Reusing a workflow or execution identifier, adding a workflow version whose
928	tag already exists for that workflow, or reusing an idempotency key across
929	different operations (within the same tenant), is a conflict. Starting an
930	execution against a missing workflow or a missing workflow version is a
931	missing resource (`404 not_found`). Migrating an execution to a missing
932	version is likewise a missing resource, while migrating a completed or
933	terminated execution is a conflict; a malformed migration body is a
934	validation error, and a migration to the version already bound is a
935	state-returning no-op rather than an error.
936	Exceeding a tenant's declared workflow or execution quota is also a `409
937	conflict`, with the word "quota" in the message so it can be distinguished
938	from an identifier conflict; the rejected request writes nothing. Referencing
939	a resource owned by another tenant is a missing resource (`404
940	not_found`), indistinguishable from one that does not exist, so existence is
941	never revealed across tenants. A `retries` value that is negative, non-integer, or greater than
942	10, and a non-positive `timeout_seconds`, are validation errors. A malformed
943	subscription — a missing or mistyped field, an unknown field, an empty or
944	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
945	a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than ten attempts — is a
946	validation error that rejects the whole request without partial writes, and
947	querying the delivery history of a missing execution is a missing resource. An approval
948	point with an empty approver list, a duplicate or non-string approver, an
949	approval on a non-task node, and a decision body that is malformed or carries
950	a decision other than `approved` or `rejected` are validation errors.
951	A decision by an approver who is
952	not listed for the pending point, or any decision against an execution that
953	has no pending approval point (other than a repeat of the decision that
954	resolved the latest one), is a conflict. Claiming a work item whose lease is
955	still active, submitting results for a work item held by another worker or
956	after the lease expired, and heartbeating or releasing a lease held by
957	another worker are conflicts, while heartbeating or releasing an execution
958	with no claimed work item is a missing resource. Recovering a missing
959	execution is a missing resource, while recovering an execution that has no
960	checkpoint or whose latest checkpoint is unparseable is a conflict; an
961	invalid recover body is a validation error. An invalid schedule declaration —
962	a non-positive or non-integer interval, a malformed or out-of-range cron
963	expression, declaring both an interval and a cron plan, an unknown missed
964	policy, or an unknown field — is a validation error that rejects the whole
965	request without partial writes; pausing, resuming, or updating the schedule
966	of a missing workflow, or pausing and resuming a workflow that has no
967	schedule, is a missing resource, and a malformed pause or resume body is a
968	validation error. Request bodies must not contain
969	non-finite numbers (`NaN`, `Infinity`, or overflowing values such as `1e400`);
970	they are rejected with 400. Finite floats keep their full precision, including negative zero
971	(`-0.0`), and every response body ends with a single newline.
972	
973	## Tests
974	
975	```bash
976	PYTHONPATH=src python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
977	```
978	
979
